extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, agents, applicants, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural rules governing patent applications, examination, continuity, amendments, abandonment, assignments, and related patent-prosecution and property issues in U.S. patent practice. Includes examiner duties, filing/part requirements, and substantive limits on amendments and claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing commences proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Filing is the commencement of proceedings to obtain a patent; an application is filed at any time after invention complete unless it is abandoned; when delivered to Patent Office with the fee it is filed; not by filing model or writing application or putting the case in hands of solicitors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An application is not accepted by the Patent Office until complete; acted on by the Office only when all parts are complete; after filing it is known by title and number; filing date and proof (date of filing how shown) matter for priority and public-use questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness and parts filing rule
rubrics_metrics.description: All parts of an application must be within two years after filing petition; parts separately filed must be accompanied with a letter connecting them with other parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If parts are filed separately the applicant must show relation; specification not withdrawn; examination proceeds in order of completion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commissioner's filing decision conclusive
rubrics_metrics.description: Decision of Commissioner as to filing is conclusive; delay in filing may be conclusive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determination that an application was filed (or filed at a certain time) rests with the Commissioner and is typically final for Patent Office procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination order and form sufficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications are examined in order of completion; the examiner should require sufficiency in form and no decision on the merits is made until all formal questions are settled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners issue notices of defects; they must state objections definitely and give the mode of avoiding them; objections to form are actionable by the applicant and must be addressed before merits are reached.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiners' duties and standards for rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner decides patentability from any data at his command according to rules of courts and Commissioner's judgments; not bound by conclusions of former examiners; must cite references and give reasons in notices of rejection; may reject if invention evidently impracticable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must state grounded reasons and cite references; they are not required to draft claim language for applicant; grounds and references that may be cited are governed by law and practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two central questions in examination
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two questions involved in application examination: (1) patentability of the invention; (2) who is the inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both patentability and inventorship may be independently litigated or decided during prosecution; examiner must consider public knowledge and legal precedents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendment substantive/form limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Amendments to the application may be partial or total and, in form, may be made to any extent; in substance an amendment cannot embrace new matter or enlarge the invention; substitute of a different specific invention for the one claimed is improper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amendments must not introduce new subject-matter; changes that effectively enlarge the invention or substitute a different invention are barred; numerous examples exist (see cited examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendment procedural requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: An amendment must be accompanied with an explanation showing how it avoids the examiner's objections; amendments cannot be made after final rejection in certain circumstances and are presumed against from delay in filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an amendment is offered the applicant should explain its purpose; new oath may be required when amendment affects inventorship or is filed by an executor; examiner may refuse to allow amendment without sufficient reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendments and claims withdrawn to avoid rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: An amendment cannot include claims once withdrawn to avoid rejection and cannot prejudice intermediate inventors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims previously withdrawn to avoid rejection cannot later be reinserted via amendment; applicants must be careful not to prejudice third-party rights by tardy amendments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity and relation to original application
rubrics_metrics.description: A continuous application takes the date of the original; it may be dependent on the original; tests of continuity exist; no presumption of priority between continuous applications except as established by rules; filing and fees rules apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuity is critical for priority as to public use and other defenses; true date, filing date proof, and how continuity is tested are important (examples and detailed tests cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification, description, and claim scope
rubrics_metrics.description: The Description and the Claim: the specification (description, drawings, or model) may show patentable matter but only the matter claimed is covered by the patent; where two specifications describe but only one claims, patent issues on the latter; disclaimers must explain the claim and not contradict it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims define the metes and bounds of the monopoly; the specification supports claims but the patent's enforceable scope is the claims as issued; disclaimers and descriptions must be consistent with claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings and models requisites
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawings and models have requisites for Patent Office submission; models and specimens may be ordered; there are rules on true date and when models/specimens are ordered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants must comply with prescribed drawing/model requirements; failure to do so can delay acceptance or examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application procedure governed by rules in force when commenced
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedure on an application is governed by the rules in force when the proceedings were commenced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This locks applications to the procedural regime in effect at filing; changes in later rules typically do not retroactively apply to pending proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misjoinder, divisionals, and joinder objections
rubrics_metrics.description: Objections for misjoinder may be made; division may be ordered and how it is made is governed by rules; cross-disclaimers and a new oath to each divisional are required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If multiple inventions are improperly joined, the examiner may require division; cross-disclaimers and procedural compliance are necessary to preserve rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeals from examiner decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions of examiners (including as to claims) may be appealed; same claims may not be inserted in a new application after appeal in certain circumstances; appeal procedure and effects are governed by statute and practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants must elect to amend, appeal, or withdraw after rejection; appeal rights and timelines are strictly regulated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Withdrawal, substitution, and abandonment effects
rubrics_metrics.description: An application may be withdrawn and a substitute filed; unreasonable delay in substitution or prosecution may show abandonment to the public; abandonment has defined effects (no legal existence after certain events; revival limited).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abandonment consequences include loss of benefit of filing date for public-use questions and potential estoppel; revival is rare and constrained (Congressional revival noted in some contexts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Abandonment to the public — grounds and computation
rubrics_metrics.description: Abandonment may occur by express acts or words, cancellation of claims, or unreasonable delay in prosecuting; not by attorney action, not by filing a new application, not by some Patent Office delays/errors; two years' inaction after last action is a common trigger; burden of proof on applicant to show non-abandonment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'last action' and 'inaction' are specifically defined; suspension of action is distinguished from inaction; computation of time (two years) and consequences are detailed, and Commissioner determinations may be conclusive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowance and issuance procedural points
rubrics_metrics.description: Allowance triggers notices; before allowance the application is under examiner control; after allowance the patent is not withdrawn from issue except by the Commissioner; a patent is not binding on the Commissioner until it issues; in some cases the Commissioner may withhold issuance (mandamus issues).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once allowed, final fees and issuance mechanics determine when rights vest; patent remains pending until official delivery/issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment form and essential content
rubrics_metrics.description: Assignments of letters-patent/patent must be written and signed by the assignor; no particular form is necessary but assignments must contain operative words purporting to convey both the invention and the monopoly; a seal is unnecessary; parol evidence cannot vary assignment terms except in mutual mistake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assignments can transfer exclusive rights to make, use, and sell; they transfer only such rights as the assignor possesses; descriptions must be intelligible though need not include full specification; assignments should be recorded to protect against intervening parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of recording and timing of assignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Recording an assignment gives legal title where there are no intervening rights and is necessary for the assignee to safely sue; without timely recording the assignee may have only equitable title and be vulnerable to subsequent purchasers or creditors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recordation within prescribed time protects against intervening transfers; an unrecorded assignment may still be valid inter partes. The date of recordation and related proofs are important evidentiary matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and limits of assignment
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignment transfers only the patented invention described in the assignment; transfer of elements of a combination does not necessarily transfer the combination patent; transfer of 'all my right' is subject to prior conveyances and generally covers only the assignor's interest unless broader words are used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties should draft assignments carefully to express intent (exclusive rights, territorial scope, future improvements, royalties, etc.). Assignments of future patents are often contracts rather than true present transfers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignee rights, remedies, and estoppel
rubrics_metrics.description: Assignee has all rights and powers of assignor, may recover profits (even when paying assignor fixed royalty), is entitled to injunctions, and is subject to equities and prior obligations of assignor; assignee may be estopped to deny validity when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assignees must evaluate prior outstanding licenses, equities, and potential defenses to infringement; remedies against assignor for defective title or warranty are available (rescission, damages, accounting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignor duties and liabilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Assignor may be estopped from denying validity of the assigned patent, may have obligations and warranties implied by consideration, and faces remedies (including actions for purchase money recovery) if assignment procured by fraud or deceit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assignors who provide express warranties or who have covenanted not to challenge validity may be limited in defenses; courts consider fairness, fraud, and statutory principles in disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and patentability criteria for 'art'
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'art' is defined by essential attributes: it must produce physical effects, may be a force applied, mode of application, or specific treatment of an object; may be new even if apparatus or product is old; must be useful and reduced to practice; mere functional description or mere employment of substances in an old art may not suffice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three classes of art exist with distinctions; combination arts have essentials; identity is shown by identity of product; patenting an art should claim it as an art, not merely as apparatus or product, to cover all modes of practicing it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims for art vs. apparatus/product
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim for an art must claim the art itself and not merely the apparatus or product; a patent for an art covers all modes of pursuing it; claims must meet requisite formal and substantive requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When drafting claims for processes or methods, ensure language captures the art and is not limited inadvertently to a particular apparatus or product unless intended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof allocation in patent litigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Burden of proof in patent cases is allocated on issues such as inventive skill, prior use, publication, utility, abandonment, specification fraud/ambiguity, excessive claims, and priority; on defendants to show patentee is not true inventor in appropriate circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties should prepare proof accordingly: patentees to prove validity and priority; defendants to prove invalidating facts or lack of inventorship, with burdens on specific elements depending on the issue.
